metadata.title: JEPA Explained: How Latent World Models Differ from VLMs

beats.narration_text: Hola, this is Hrishikesh. Today we tear down JEPA, the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture proposed by Yann LeCun and Meta AI, and explain how predicting in abstract representation space fundamentally differs from traditional Vision-Language Models and pixel decoders.

props.command: explain JEPA (I-JEPA & V-JEPA) and contrast latent representation prediction with traditional Vision-Language Models.
props.runningText: comparing token/pixel generative objectives against abstract latent prediction...
output: ✓ Predicts in abstract latent space s_y, not raw pixels or text tokens
✓ EMA Target Encoder + Stop-Gradient prevents collapse without negatives
✓ I-JEPA reaches 79.3% ImageNet linear probe & V-JEPA hits 71.4% on SSv2

beats.narration_text: Traditional Vision-Language Models compress images into text-aligned tokens, while generative autoencoders reconstruct every pixel. Both hit a wall: pixels waste capacity on random noise, and captions discard three-D physics. JEPA predicts masked semantics directly in latent space.

props.text:
Visual Representation Hypothesis
To understand the world, a vision model
must reconstruct pixels or map to text.
Pixel decoders waste compute on surface noise,
and text captions discard 3D motion physics.
JEPA predicts masked semantics in latent space.
props.triggerWords: reconstruct pixels or map to text

beats.narration_text: Compare the two architectural topologies side by side. Where generative VLMs and Masked Autoencoders pass embeddings through a heavy token or pixel decoder, JEPA pairs a context encoder and an exponential-moving-average target encoder with a narrow latent predictor.

Why does prediction space matter? A pixel decoder minimizes error over exact RGB values, forcing the network to memorize stochastic leaf textures and water ripples. A text VLM only learns what humans write in captions. JEPA's target encoder filters out unpredictable pixel detail.

props.command: compare the mathematical objective, modality grounding, and collapse prevention of JEPA vs. CLIP/LLaVA and MAE.
props.runningText: analyzing information bottlenecks across pixel, text, and latent spaces...
output: ✓ Generative/MAE: ||Decoder(f(x)) - y||^2 models unpredictable pixel noise
✓ Traditional VLM: -sum log P(w_t | w_<t, Proj(f(x))) drops 3D physics
✓ JEPA: ||Pred(f(x), z) - sg(f_ema(y))||^2 predicts high-level semantics

beats.narration_text: In I-JEPA's forward pass, the context encoder processes only visible patches, while the target encoder embeds the full image under stop-gradient and layer normalization. The predictor takes context tokens plus positional mask tokens to regress the masked target embeddings.

props.code:
# I-JEPA Latent Step
with torch.no_grad():
  s_y = target_enc(img)
  s_y = mask_target(
    s_y, target_masks
  )
s_x = ctx_enc(img, ctx_m)
s_hat = predictor(
  s_x, pos_tokens
)
loss = l1_loss(s_hat, s_y)
# EMA: m*t_enc + (1-m)*c_enc

beats.narration_text: On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA reaches seventy-nine point three percent linear probe accuracy with ViT-Huge in under twelve hundred GPU hours—up to ten times faster than Masked Autoencoders—while beating MAE by six point three points on one-percent low-shot ImageNet and DINO by ten point one points on CLEVR depth.

What breaks a Joint-Embedding architecture? Because both encoders map into latent space, a symmetric network minimizes L-two loss by outputting a constant zero vector everywhere. JEPA avoids representation collapse using an asymmetric EMA target encoder and large multi-block masks.

props.text:
Representation Collapse & Masking Trap
A naive joint-embedding network with L2 loss
naturally converges to rich semantic features.
Symmetric encoders output zero everywhere.
JEPA requires an asymmetric EMA stop-gradient
and large semantic multi-block target masks.
props.triggerWords: naturally converges to rich semantic features

beats.narration_text: When extended to video in V-JEPA, the gap with text-trained VLMs becomes unmistakable. On Kinetics-400 static recognition, OpenCLIP-G and V-JEPA score near eighty percent, but on Something-Something-v2 temporal physics, OpenCLIP collapses to thirty-five point eight percent while V-JEPA reaches seventy-one point four percent.

Look at the multi-block masking collator that makes I-JEPA and V-JEPA work. By sampling four large target blocks covering fifteen to twenty percent of the frame and stripping overlapping patches from the context, the predictor cannot interpolate local edges and must infer object geometry.

props.code:
# Multi-Block Masking
def sample_masks():
  # M=4 target blocks
  # scale: 15% to 20%
  t_m = [
    block(0.15, 0.20)
    for _ in range(4)
  ]
  # Context: 85%-100%
  c_m = block(0.85, 1.0)
  c_m = strip(c_m, t_m)
  return c_m, t_m

beats.narration_text: JEPA does not replace language models; it supplies the grounded physical world model that text-bottlenecked VLMs lack. Use traditional VLMs for OCR and semantic Q-and-A, and deploy JEPA backbones when three-D geometry, sample efficiency, and physical motion govern. Your turn.
